sections.text: A note in Emacs and a page on the web serve different purposes. The useful question is not whether they look identical, but whether the structure, examples, and connections that make the note useful survive the journey. This guide connects two working examples in the notebook. Start with the publishing fixture to inspect individual features, then read the Rust article to see those features supporting an explanation. Inspect the publishing surface Read an example in context Keep the connections in the source Read another author’s workflow Questions to explore next

sections.heading: Inspect the publishing surface
sections.text: The Org-mode publishing showcase deliberately puts headings, tables, task states, inline formatting, and source blocks together. It is the place to look when asking a narrow question: does this part of an Org document still make sense after export? The route here is Org → ox-hugo Markdown → Berlin’s semantic document → HTML. Each stage has a different responsibility. Emacs remains the authoring environment; the published page does not reproduce folding, agendas, or capture workflows. The showcase documents examples, not a promise of support for every Org feature.

sections.heading: Read an example in context
sections.text: Processing JSON with Rust is a learning exercise rather than a publishing test. Read it for the relationship between the prose, the source listings, and the medal results. Code references let an explanation point to a precise part of a listing without turning the whole article into a wall of code. The worked medal pipeline also makes a useful distinction visible: showing the steps of an execution is not the same as executing a program in the reader’s browser. Stored Org results can accompany source code; Berlin’s publishing export does not execute the code blocks again.

sections.heading: Keep the connections in the source
sections.text: The links above are Org ID links. Their targets are document identities, not hand-maintained HTML filenames. Berlin resolves them against the published collection and derives backlinks to the passages that refer to each note. That division keeps two different kinds of organisation separate. Tags gather material with shared labels. A guide chooses a route through that material and explains why each stop belongs. The explanation remains ordinary prose, so it can change as the notebook grows.

sections.heading: Read another author’s workflow
sections.text: Dominik Honnef’s My org-roam workflows for taking notes and writing articles describes a broader system connecting notes, references, and web publication. His use of category notes is especially relevant here: a category can contain an explanation as well as collect links. It offers a useful comparison, not a description of the configuration used by this website.

sections.heading: Questions to explore next
sections.text: These two questions are starting points for further investigation, not completed experiments. Each connects something already in the notebook to a small next step.

sections.heading: What would make a stored result reproducible?
sections.text: The worked example in Processing JSON with Rust places a small input beside its extraction, counting, and ranking results. That makes the explanation inspectable. It does not, by itself, establish that another environment will produce the same result. The uncertainty is what needs to accompany the stored output: the exact input, source listings, dependency lockfile, Rust toolchain, and execution command are a starting point. Is that enough to reproduce this particular example? A small experiment would be to use a disposable copy of the example, record those inputs, and compare a fresh execution with the stored table. Then change one medal in the small input and regenerate the results. Record what changed and whether the explanation still matches. Run this explicitly during authoring; the publishing export should continue to use stored results. The useful follow-up would be a short note containing the recorded setup, comparison, and any mismatch—not a claim of reproducibility before trying it.

sections.heading: Where should a guide end and a note begin?
sections.text: This guide introduces both the publishing showcase and the Rust learning exercise. The uncertainty is how much orientation belongs here without repeating the explanations in those notes. A small reading exercise would be to follow the links with two different questions: “Which Org features can I inspect?” and “How do code references support an explanation?” For each route, record the first place where context is missing or unnecessarily repeated. Put route-finding context in the guide and keep the technical explanation beside its example. The result may be only a revised paragraph or a better link. A separate note is useful when there is an observation worth explaining, not just to fill out the collection.

I write in Emacs Org-mode. This page is where I check what happens to that writing on its way to the web: Org source is exported by ox-hugo to Markdown, then parsed and rendered by Berlin. It is both a public example and a publishing fixture. The deliberately deep headings, task states, tables, and code blocks give me a varied document to inspect when I change the pipeline. This is not a claim of complete Org-mode support; it is a place to make the current behavior visible. What to look for This is an example headline Another headline Basic markup Showing and hiding headlines Tables Org-mode links Various things you can add in headers The TODO-planner payoff Exporting an org-mode buffer Further authoring features and source blocks

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.text: Structure: nested headings and lists should remain understandable outside Emacs, including where the exporter turns deep outlines into lists. Inline content: emphasis, verbatim text, and links should preserve their meaning and remain readable. Tables and tasks: compare the table layout, checkboxes, task labels, tags, and priority markers in the examples below. Code and stored results: source blocks should be readable as listings. Publishing does not execute them; any displayed results are already present in the Org source. Folding, agenda views, capture commands, and keyboard shortcuts belong to the Emacs authoring experience. Describing them here does not make them interactive features of this static page. Some export-specific material, such as LaTeX, may need additional handling rather than appearing exactly as it does in Emacs. The examples below were retained from an introductory document described as the example file for a Denver Emacs Org-mode talk. They remain useful as a varied publishing fixture; the talk-oriented examples are not a description of my personal setup. For these publishing features in a regular article, see Processing JSON with Rust. That link also exercises the resolution of an Org ID into a published page.

Next, let's talk about some markup underscores let you underline things stars add emphasis slashes are italics pluses are strikethrough equal signs are verbatim text tildes can also be used You can generate lists with the - character (seen above), or create numbered ones: Number one thing Number two thing Number three

sections.heading: Showing and hiding headlines
sections.text: You can hide the contents of a headline by putting the point (cursor) or it and hitting TAB. You can also toggle hiding and showing of all headlines with SHIFT-TAB.

sections.heading: Tables
sections.text: Auto expanding tables are one of the coolest features of org-mode, because tables in Markdown just plain suck. In order to create a new table, you can start typing it manually, or press C-c |, which will prompt for the table's dimensions. First Name Last Name Years using Emacs Lee Hinman 5 Mike Hunsinger 2 Daniel Glauser 4 Really-long-first-name-guy long-last-name-pers 1

sections.heading: Org-mode links
sections.text: :PROPERTIES:... In an org-mode file, you can press C-c l to store a pointer to wherever you are in the file. Then, with (or without) text highlighted hit C-C C-l to make it into a link. The example file for Magit If you don't want to store a pointer (ie, link to a website or something), you can just hit C-c C-l and type or paste the link. To manually create a link, do something like: The Denver Emacs Meetup Group Writequit site Google's web site Google (ignore the *_SRC blocks for now, we'll get there) [[http://google.com/][Google]] You can link to files, images, websites, emails, irc, and all kinds of things.

sections.heading: Various things you can add in headers
sections.text: One of the most common uses for org-mode is a sort of "task list" or TODO list. Org-mode supports this by allowing markers in the headline for the state of a task. Let's look at an example:

sections.heading: TODO This is a task that needs doing
TODO Another todo task
sections.text: sub task one sub task two sub task three

sections.heading: TODO learn other stuff
sections.text: You can toggle each task in a list with the C-c C-c keyboard shortcut.

sections.heading: DONE I've already finished this one
sections.text: You can change the status of a task by hitting C-c t in the body of a task anywhere, which will prompt for the state to put it in. You can create as many of these as you'd like, for example (from my own config, use what works best for you, configuring them is a little out of scope right here) here's what I use:

sections.heading: WAITING waiting for someone else before doing anything
NEEDSREVIEW there's a PR for this, it needs someone to look at it
HOLD this is in permanent hold until further notice
CANCELLED I don't need this any more
SOMEDAY I'd like to do this someday in the waaaaay off future
sections.text: A lot of people just use "TODO" and "DONE" though.

sections.heading: The TODO-planner payoff
sections.text: :PROPERTIES:... So TODOs are all well and good, but what is a really neat feature is when you can easily capture new TODOs and display them easily. In order to do this, let's configure a couple of Emacs options in your emacs init: (require 'org) ;; Setup C-c c to capture new TODOs (global-set-key (kbd "C-c c") 'org-capture) ;; Setup a key bind for the agenda (global-set-key (kbd "C-c a") 'org-agenda) ;; Set up agenda to know about our file, you can use a list of files or ;; directories here (setq org-agenda-files '("~/todo.org")) ;; A new template (setq org-capture-templates '(("t" "Todo" entry (file "~/todo.org") "* TODO %?\n%U\n"))) Now, hit C-c c to bring up the capture template list, then t to capture a new TODO item. Once you've captured a few TODOs, you can try out the agenda by hitting C-c a, which will prompt for what agenda you'd like to see, for now hit t to see the TODO list agenda.

sections.heading: Exporting an org-mode buffer
sections.text: Org has a lot of export options, they are all contained behind a C-c C-e export backend, exporting to HTML, markdown, plain text, pdf, etc.

As I’ve been learning Rust, I’ve been looking for easy and practical projects to get my head around basic concepts and increase my syntax muscle memory. One of the more common tasks is to load data from different sources, like text files, or more structured data like JSON. So it got me thinking, how would parsing a fairly complex JSON look like in Rust? Luckily, it is not this difficult! The code Let's add indexing operations Conclusion Next Steps This post is a demonstration of using serde_json to parse JSON in Rust. For this purpose, I am using the athletics data set of the Olympic Games Tokyo 2020. The goal is to find the five most successful countries and print them. Print the top five countries and the medals they won. United States of America MedalCount { g: 7, s: 12, b: 7 } Italy MedalCount { g: 5, s: 0, b: 0 } Kenya MedalCount { g: 4, s: 4, b: 2 } Poland MedalCount { g: 4, s: 2, b: 3 } Jamaica MedalCount { g: 4, s: 1, b: 4 } Org-mode publishing showcase I chose an excerpt of the athletics data set, because its a bit more complex than a typical hello world example. The data set is deeply nested, contains a lot of data and different object types and to make things even more interesting some data, such as the countryObject field appears to be inconsistent. Figure 1: Structure of our JSON data The expanded path runs through pageProps, gameDiscipline, events, awards, and participant to countryObject. Open the full-size JSON tree In order to print the requested information, we need to parse the JSON data and extract the fields medalType and the countryObejct as shown above. A detail in the data countryObject is not always an object. The lookup tests is_object() before choosing the field and otherwise falls back to country. See the country lookup

sections.heading: The code
sections.text: Serde_json allows us to map JSON data to enums and this is what we are going to do. Since we also want to count the different types of medals we define a struct called MedalCount. #[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, Deserialize)] enum Class { #[serde(rename = "GOLD")] Gold, #[serde(rename = "SILVER")] Silver, #[serde(rename = "BRONZE")] Bronze, } #[derive(Default, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)] struct MedalCount { g: usize, s: usize, b: usize, }

sections.heading: Let's add indexing operations
sections.text: Thanks to serde_json we can easily map the medal data to our enum. But how can we use this information to our advantage once we want to count how many gold, silver and bronze medals a country won? After all, we would like to keep the actual counting as readable as possible and for this, the mapping logic needs be stored elsewhere. Luckily, Rust offers two traits that can be used for indexing operations: Index and IndexMut. By implementing both traits we can map a variant of our class enum to the respective field in our MedalCount struct as shown below. impl Index<Class> for MedalCount { type Output = usize; fn index(&self, class: Class) -> &Self::Output { match class { Class::Gold => &self.g, Class::Silver => &self.s, Class::Bronze => &self.b, } } } impl IndexMut<Class> for MedalCount { fn index_mut(&mut self, class: Class) -> &mut Self::Output { match class { Class::Gold => &mut self.g, Class::Silver => &mut self.s, Class::Bronze => &mut self.b, } } } As far as I know, serde_json does not support mapping of nested data to struct via some form of dot notation. Luckily, if data is not mapped to a predefined struct than the JSON data can still be deserialized into a Value, which then allows us to get the nested data we want. Follow the three operations in this listing: Extract country names, count medals, and rank the results. fn get_class_country_tuple<'a>(values: &'a Vec<Value>) -> Vec<(Class, String)> { let get_country = |participant: &'a serde_json::Value| -> &'a serde_json::Value { let mut country_key = "countryObject"; if !participant[country_key].is_object() { country_key = "country"; } &participant[country_key]["name"] }; let to_tuple = |v: &'a Value| { let class = serde_json::from_value::<Class>(v["medalType"].to_owned()).unwrap(); let country = get_country(&v["participant"]).as_str().unwrap().to_string(); (class, country) }; values.iter().map(to_tuple).collect() } // returns a projection on the medals per country data pub fn get_medals_per_country(&self) -> Result<Projection, Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let to_medal_country_tuple = |v: &serde_json::Value| get_class_country_tuple(v["awards"].as_array().unwrap()); let group_by_country = |mut acc: HashMap<_, _>, x| { let (class, country): (Class, String) = x; // remember the IndexMut trait, we used it here for indexing // If there is no entry for a country yet, we create one and // initialize the medal count to g: 0, s: 0, b: 0. // The fields will be incremented by one based on the indexing // operations defined earlier. // So, the value "Gold" will be deserialized to the enum variant // Class::Gold which will increment the field `g` of teh struct // MedalCount. acc.entry(country).or_insert(MedalCount::default())[class] += 1; acc }; let events = self.0.json["pageProps"]["gameDiscipline"]["events"] .as_array() .unwrap(); let mut medals_per_country = events .into_iter() .flat_map(to_medal_country_tuple) .fold(HashMap::new(), group_by_country) .into_iter() .collect::<Vec<(_, _)>>(); medals_per_country.sort_by(|a, b| b.1.cmp(&a.1)); Ok(Projection(medals_per_country)) } Extract the country name. The lookup uses countryObject when it is an object, otherwise country. Accumulate the medals. Each country gets a counter; IndexMut selects the gold, silver, or bronze field to increment. Rank the results. The comparison orders by gold first, then silver, then bronze—not by the total medal count. #[derive(Eq, PartialEq)] struct Projection(Vec<(String, MedalCount)>); impl Projection { fn empty() -> Self { Self(vec![]) } fn take(self, n: usize) -> Self { Self(self.0.into_iter().take(n).collect()) } fn get(&self) -> &Vec<(String, MedalCount)> { &self.0 } } Having all the components in place, we can finally implement the logic we wanted: fn load_data() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> { let url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/sekaiser/rust-sample-parse-json/main/athletics.json"; let db = AthleticsDb::from_url(Url::from_str(url)?)?; let mut last_top5 = Projection::empty(); loop { let medals_per_country = db.get_medals_per_country()?; let top5 = medals_per_country.take(5); if top5 != last_top5 { for e in top5.get() { println!("{} {:?}", e.0, e.1); } last_top5 = top5; } thread::sleep(time::Duration::from_secs(2)); } } { "pageProps": {"gameDiscipline": {"events": [ {"awards": [ {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"countryObject":{"name":"Japan"}}}, {"medalType":"SILVER","participant":{"country":{"name":"Italy"}}}, {"medalType":"BRONZE","participant":{"country":{"name":"Italy"}}}, {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"countryObject":{"name":"Japan"}}}, {"medalType":"GOLD","participant":{"country":{"name":"Kenya"}}} ]} ]}} } Japan → gold Italy → silver Italy → bronze Japan → gold Kenya → gold Japan: gold 2, silver 0, bronze 0 Italy: gold 0, silver 1, bronze 1 Kenya: gold 1, silver 0, bronze 0 1. Japan — 2 gold 2. Kenya — 1 gold 3. Italy — 1 silver, 1 bronze

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This post demonstrates the usage of serde_json in order to parse nested JSON data. The article also briefly covers how to use traits in order to keep the code organized and the logic clean. Serde is very powerful and I encourage people who are interested in Rust to take a look at it.
